subject: history
title: Reformation Foundations of the European Witch Craze
welcome_lead: Why early modern Europe came to believe in a Satanic conspiracy.
meta_desc: A-Level Witch Craze adventure on Reformation context, demonologies and patterns of European prosecution c.1580-1620.
final_note: You can connect religious upheaval to the demonological worldview.

concepts.def: 1487 inquisitorial manual by Kramer (and Sprenger) codifying witch-hunting procedure; widely reprinted by Protestants and Catholics.
Theological doctrine of demons and witches as Satan's agents; central to early modern witch-belief.
Allegation that witches signed a personal covenant with Satan, distinguishing learned demonology from popular maleficium.
Harmful magic causing illness, crop failure or death, the popular core of witch accusations.
Confessional uncertainty and apocalyptic expectation after Luther (1517) intensifying fears of the devil's activity.
Treatise by James VI of Scotland defending witch belief and the use of judicial torture; reissued in England in 1603.

walkthroughs.body_html: Late-medieval ideas of demonic conspiracy crystallised in the Malleus Maleficarum (1487). The Carolina Code (1532) introduced inquisitorial procedure in the Holy Roman Empire. Both Catholic and Protestant authorities accepted that the devil empowered witches. Confessional rivalry sharpened fear after the Council of Trent (1545-63) and the Augsburg Settlement (1555).

Prosecutions clustered in the Holy Roman Empire (~25,000 of an estimated 40,000-50,000 European executions). Trier (1581-93), Fulda (1603-06) and Würzburg (1626-31) produced mass burnings. Scotland's North Berwick trials (1590-91), supervised by King James VI, accused witches of plotting against the king; James's Daemonologie (1597) followed.

Cold summers in the 1580s and 1590s, harvest failures and the Thirty Years' War (1618-48) fed fears of supernatural sabotage. Local notables, clergy and judges combined accusation, torture and confession. Sabbath narratives - night flights and demonic gatherings - spread through pamphlets, sermons and printed trial accounts.
